rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec hike ~82% (from ~79% overnight); ECB Dec ~89% (Nov 4); BoJ Dec ~80%; BoC Dec ~35%; RBNZ Dec <50%; BoE 4.00% and RBA 4.85% after November hikes
rows.read: A December Federal Reserve hike is still the market's main expectation, and two Fed presidents leaned that way on Monday, which keeps rate support under the dollar. Hikes are also expected in Europe and Japan, while job losses in Canada and New Zealand, and now cheaper oil, give those banks reasons to wait. Tuesday's US inflation figures are the next big check.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: US payrolls +165K (fcst 65K); Canada unemployment 6.7%; NZ 5.7%; China Oct CPI 0.7% y/y; China 24% tariff pause extended to Jan 10; UK Q3 GDP Thu 1:00 AM CT, fcst +0.7% q/q
rows.read: The US job market looks much firmer than Canada's or New Zealand's, a split that favours the US dollar. China extended its tariff truce with the US to January, which removes a near-term risk for the Aussie and the kiwi, though Chinese shoppers remain cautious. UK growth figures on Thursday are the next big read.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: NY Fed 1-yr inflation expectations 3.9% (Oct); US Sep CPI +0.6% m/m, Oct due Tue 7:30 AM CT (fcst +0.3%, core +0.2%); China PPI 5.7% y/y; Brent ~$95
rows.read: Cheaper oil is easing fears that the energy shock keeps feeding prices, which helped gold and the euro. But Americans still expect prices to rise fast over the next year, and Fed officials see the AI building boom adding to price pressure. Tuesday's US figures will show whether inflation is cooling; hot prices would favour the dollar.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.figure: NZD/USD +1.6%, AUD/USD +0.8%, EUR/CHF +0.7%; US 3-year auction high yield 4.627%, weakest bid-to-cover of 2026
rows.read: Stocks kept recovering from last week's AI and chip-stock slump, and hopes for a Hormuz deal eased war fears. Money left safe havens like the franc and moved into the kiwi and the Aussie. One wobble is weak demand at a US government bond sale, which keeps borrowing costs high.

rows.title: Terms of Trade
rows.figure: Brent ~$94.99 (−3.4%), WTI ~$87.20 (−4.0%); Brent $116.72 at the Oct 30 close; Saudi East-West pipeline hit, output unaffected
rows.read: Oil fell about 3% on reports of an Iranian offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, though no deal is signed. That cuts the energy bill for importers like Japan and the euro area. It also takes support from the Canadian dollar, which stood still while most currencies rose.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: CFTC Nov 3: hedge funds for USD, JPY, AUD, GBP; against NZD (19th percentile), CAD (21st), EUR (35th); 4-week change NZD −22K, EUR −34K contracts; real money very bearish GBP and AUD
rows.read: Hedge funds lean toward the dollar and the yen and against the kiwi, the Canadian dollar and the euro, and over the past month they sharply added to their bets against the kiwi and the euro. In the Aussie and the pound, hedge funds and real-money investors sit on opposite sides, with real money betting heavily against both.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: NZ governing bloc 67 of 131 seats, official result Nov 27; Democrats control House and Senate; France on negative outlook at Moody's; US 3-year auction weak (bid-to-cover 2.53)
rows.read: No new budget news moved currencies today. New Zealand's election count points to the same coalition staying, which lowers the risk of a big budget change and helped the kiwi. A Democratic Congress still makes President Trump's spending plans harder to pass, a mild drag on the dollar.
